title: What I Talk About When I Talk to My Children about Spelling
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. recounts how he coaches his own daughters through weekly spelling-list practice during their morning drive to school, framing the practice not as a scholastic obligation but as an application of his Five Key Beliefs framework for motivation at home. He opens by insisting his children's worth isn't tied to academic performance, then describes a simple oral quiz-and-feedback routine he uses in the car. He explains how he layers Credibility (showing he cares and sharing memory tricks), Value (framing spelling as inherently enjoyable rather than useful), Effort and Efficacy (leveraging the testing effect and pointing to measurable gains), and Belonging (helping his kids identify as people who learn from mistakes, not as good or bad spellers) into the routine. The piece functions as a parenting story about building a low-stakes, high-connection practice habit with his own children rather than a classroom lesson plan for other teachers.
points: Stuart uses simple oral retrieval practice (reading words aloud, having his daughters spell them, looping back to missed words) rather than any curriculum or app, showing how low-tech the testing effect can be applied at home.
He explicitly avoids emphasizing spelling's future utility with his children, arguing that framing learning around enjoyment of improvement sustains motivation better than utility arguments.
He models how to defuse a child's over-identification with a single test score by separating self-worth from performance ("it's just a test result. It's not you.").
The piece documents a measurable outcome — his daughters' pretest scores rose from 50-60% to 80-95% — as evidence that a few minutes of consistent retrieval practice compounds over time.
quotes: I have no dreams of my children being top in their class or "exceptional" in any other way that the world measures. This is because I know what is true: that they are exceptional just as they are.

When they first started at the school, my daughters felt stressed about these lists and didn't do very well on them. When I learned of this, I told them not to fret and that we'd start to use our drive time to school to practice the lists.

Value: I try to emphasize to my children that it's fun to get better at spelling. I don't talk to them AT ALL about how they'll "use" spelling someday because I want them to see that education is about so much more than its utility.

As we've gone, they've both shifted from 50-60% on pretests to 80-95%, and I've taken care to gently point them toward how their consistent, simple effort — the car-ride testing — has led to these results.

Whenever I do sense them putting too much identification with the score, I push against that: "Woah, that test result seemed to really bug you. How come? … Well listen, it's just a test result. It's not you. You're great.
